query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX HEAs operated at >900 °C in oxidizing or corrosive environments, the element X controls the formation of a protective surface oxide by mediating its diffusion kinetics and oxidation pathway. When X = Al, its slow diffusion leads to a controlled, continuous formation of a coherent α‐Al2O3 layer that grows slowly and adheres well; when X = Mn, its higher diffusivity and tendency to form higher‐volume, non‐coherent oxides results in a rapidly growing, porous scale prone to cracking or spallation; and for X = Si, an intermediate behavior is expected with the potential formation of a protective silicate or glassy oxide layer.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state) with X = Al, Mn, or Si, prepared to ensure homogeneous elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy samples to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for an extended period (e.g., 100 hours).
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (above 900 °C) in an oxygen-rich or corrosive atmosphere; testing should maintain identical conditions (temperature, atmosphere composition, and exposure duration) across alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The nature of the surface oxide scale—its phase composition, coherency, and continuity—mediates the protective behavior. Specifically, the formation of a continuous α‐Al2O3 scale in Al-containing alloys versus a porous, cracked oxide scale in Mn-containing alloys.
generation.mechanism: The relative diffusion kinetics of the alloying element X controls the oxidation pathway at the alloy/oxide interface. In Al-doped alloys, limited Al diffusion supports the nucleation and lateral growth of a coherent, slowly thickening α‐Al2O3 scale that acts as a barrier to further oxidation. In contrast, rapid diffusion of Mn results in fast, volumetrically inconsistent oxidation producing non-coherent, spall-prone manganese oxides. Si is anticipated to yield an intermediate rate, potentially forming a protective but less robust silicate layer.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature, oxidizing conditions, alloys with X = Al should develop thin, coherent, slow-growing oxide scales exhibiting minimal cracking or spallation. Alloys with X = Mn are predicted to display thicker, rapidly growing oxide layers with a high propensity for cracking and spallation, while alloys with X = Si should show an intermediate oxide scale behavior.
generation.baseline: A CrFeCoNi alloy lacking the additional element X, which is expected to exhibit less effective oxide scale formation due to the absence of a passivating element.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys exposed above 900 °C in oxygen-rich or corrosive atmospheres. Behavior may differ at lower temperatures or in inert environments, and microstructural nuances (e.g., phase distribution) may influence the observed outcomes.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative differences in diffusion rates and oxide growth kinetics are sensitive to processing history and slight compositional variations, and the protective nature of a silicate-based layer (for X = Si) may vary with stoichiometry and local phase equilibria.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of CrFeCoNiX HEA samples (with X = Al, Mn, Si) along with a CrFeCoNi baseline alloy. Subject each sample to identical high-temperature oxidation tests in an oxygen-rich (or controlled corrosive) atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for a fixed time (e.g., 100 hours). Comparative analysis of the oxide scale thickness, morphology, phase, and adherence will be performed.
measurements: Mass change per unit area (to assess oxidation kinetics)
Cross-sectional SEM/TEM imaging to measure oxide scale thickness and examine coherency/adherence
XRD analysis for phase identification of the oxide layers
Visual and microscopic inspection for cracking, spallation, and porosity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly thinner, more coherent and adherent oxide scale compared to the baseline, or if the Mn-containing alloy does not show a notably thicker, porous, and spalling oxide scale under identical conditions, then the hypothesized mechanism linking element-specific diffusion kinetics to oxide scale stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA was successfully fabricated through the arc-melting process, with an emphasis on phase, microstructure, and real-time oxidation behaviour in two different non-ambient (high-temperature and low-oxygen partial pressure) conditions. The main findings of this research work can be summarised as follows. In a vacuum (4.2 × 10−6 atm), only MnO, a halite-type oxide, was formed during in situ oxidation, contrary to ThermoCalc’s prediction of both halite and spinel oxides, and Ni/Co forming halite. In air (1.0 atm), vigorous oxidation was observed, with most of the oxides formed being spinel. Mn remained important in the formation of spinel oxides, and Co was predicted to form spinel oxides by ThermoCalc but was not found in oxide-forming elements. Oxides like Cr2O3, Fe2O3, and Fe3O4 were not detected during in situ HTXRD in either vacuum or air, which contrasts with previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. Mn was found to be a higher oxide-forming element, producing non-protective oxides, and leading to the depletion of Mn in the bulk alloy beneath the oxide layer. At temperatures exceeding 500 °C, the oxidation behavior of traditional and complex alloys (e.g., Ni-Cr, Ni-based superalloys, Fe-Cr, CoCrFeNiMn ‘Cantor’ alloy) has been extensively studied in oxygen-rich environments and over extended periods (from days to hundreds of days,). Key contributors to the process include species transport to the oxide/metal junction within the base alloy, movement across the oxide/metal interface, and passage through the oxide layer. For instance, atmospheric oxidation of CoCrFeNiMn-containing alloys results in a layered oxide film, with Cr-rich inner and Mn-rich outer oxides attributed to outward cation diffusion. In a study by Kim et al., the high-temperature oxidation of FeCrMnNiCo (900–1100 °C in 20% O2/80% N2 for 24 h) showed the formation of layered Cr2O3 and Mn2O3 oxides at 900 °C. This process led to Ni, Fe, and Co enrichment in the base alloy. At 1000–1100 °C, the outer Mn2O3 layer changed to Mn3O4, forming a (Mn, Cr)3O4 ternary oxide with Ni, Fe, and Co in a solid solution. In the alloy OHC3, the volume fraction of NbAl3 was high but the alloy did not suffer from pest oxidation. It formed an external scale (external oxidation) and an IOZ. The external scale was composed of an outer and an inner part with different oxides according to location. In the former, the AlNbO4, CrNbO4 and αAl2O3 oxides were observed, in the latter only the αAl2O3 was found (Figure 7). The NbAl3 formed the AlNbO4 (assumed to be a result of transient oxidation) above an inner Al2O3 layer in contact with the alloy (substrate). The Laves phase formed the CrNbO4 with an inner Al2O3 layer. In some areas of the alloy/scale interface the inner continuous Al2O3 layer was not formed, instead internal oxidation had occurred where alumina oxide was observed. Internal oxidation had occurred in all facets of the cubic specimen and was deeper along the phase boundaries (Figure 8). The internal oxidation is known to cause embrittlement of the substrate and to play a role in scale spallation. At 800 °C the integrity of the scale on OHC3 was practically intact.
